title: Efficacy and the Brain 101 (David Reese Guest Post) teacher, December 15, 2023
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
source: Dave Stuart Jr. (davestuartjr.com) — guest post by David Reese ("DTR"), high school English
summary: In this rare guest post, high-school English teacher David Reese (DTR) explains how he uses a unit he calls "BRAIN 101" to make the abstract Five Key Belief of Efficacy concrete for ninth graders. Drawing on neuroscientist Richard Davidson's point that learning and emotion are enmeshed, Reese has students memorize the basics of the limbic system, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala hijack using acronyms, mnemonic "theme songs," and repeated low- and high-stakes quizzing. The heart of the piece is a case study of a student named Aaron, who takes the BRAIN 101 quiz three times, watches his score climb from a D- to an A, and is guided through a reflection process that makes the growth an "anchor experience" for believing in his own agency. Reese argues that this kind of lived, trackable progress — not a lecture about mindset — is what actually teaches students they possess efficacy. The post closes with a sample from an advanced class memorizing a full Shakespearean sonnet, offered as a parallel example of engineered, repetition-based mastery.
points: Reese ties the abstract Efficacy belief to concrete, trackable data: having students graph and reflect on three attempts at the same quiz turns "I can improve" from a slogan into a felt, evidenced experience.
The unit deliberately uses low-stakes "throw-away" quizzes alongside graded ones so students get repeated retrieval practice without the anxiety of every attempt counting toward a grade.

Memory devices (acronyms, assigned "theme songs" for brain regions) are used as scaffolding for memorization, not as the end goal — the real target is the belief shift that comes from watching effort produce results.

Reese's own admission that he "hated reading" as a student and only discovered value in college grounds his pedagogy in personal experience with disengagement, giving the efficacy argument extra credibility.
quotes: This sentence is kind of a big deal because educational neuroscientist Richard Davidson says that learning and emotions are enmeshed. Like it or not, we can't separate emotions from learning.

If I want my curriculum to matter (because time is precious), I need to make it count. If I want to make it count, it better have value, and it's not enough for me to see the value of the curriculum. The students need to see the value.
BRAIN 101 requires students to know about two crucial regions of the brain (the limbic system and prefrontal cortex) and the phenomenon we call amygdala hijack.
After twenty years of teaching, I've finally learned that if I want my students to know certain stuff, I need to make the stuff accessible.
Taking a somewhat challenging quiz (or test) multiple times provides us with the opportunity to track our progress. And this is where AGENCY, or EFFICACY, comes into play.
As you can see, Aaron has taken the BRAIN 101 quiz three times (not counting the various throw-away quizzes). On Sept 14th he scored a 3.6 (D-); on Sept 21st a 4.25 (D+).
I want students to KNOW that they possess agency. That they have efficacy. That they possess the ability to have an effect on an outcome.
